Multinomial probit regression

Source: R/estimators.R
mnprobit.Rd

Fits the multinomial probit (Hausman and Wise 1978; Daganzo 1979): utilities \(U_{ij} = V_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}\) with multivariate normal errors whose covariance is estimated, so that any pattern of correlation and heteroskedasticity across alternatives, and hence any substitution pattern, is admitted.

Usage

mnprobit(
  formula,
  data,
  id = NULL,
  alt = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  fe = NULL,
  se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"),
  cluster = NULL,
  nboot = 200L,
  cores = 1L,
  start = NULL,
  maxit = 1000L,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  draws = 200L
)

Arguments

formula

A formula; see the section "Two data layouts" of mnl().

data

A data frame.

id, alt

For the long layout, the names of the case and alternative columns of data. Leave both NULL for the wide layout.

ref

The base (reference) alternative: a level of the response. Default: the first level.

weights

Optional frequency weights: a column name in data or a numeric vector with one entry per row (constant within a case in the long layout).

offset

Optional offset on the utility scale: in the long layout a column name or a vector with one entry per row; in the wide layout an \(n \times J\) matrix (columns in level order).

fe

Optional column name in data identifying units that receive alternative-specific fixed effects.

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (inverse observed information, default), "opg" (inverse outer product of the scores, the BHHH form that mlogit reports for the nested logit and HEV), "robust", "cluster" (needs cluster), "bootstrap" (nonparametric over cases, or over clusters when cluster is given, with nboot refits from the full-sample estimate; the replicates are kept in object$boot and confint() can report percentile intervals), or "none". With fe, the bootstrap resamples units (a unit drawn twice counts as two units, each with its own fixed effects; a case bootstrap would give units random numbers of cases and a second incidental-parameters bias) and covers the slopes only: the alternative-specific constants and the unit dummies refer to reference units that change between replicates, so their bootstrap standard errors are NA, and first_difference() refuses intervals that need them (use analytic, robust, or cluster standard errors for those). A replicate whose fixed effects cannot be built (an alternative left unconnected to the base) counts as failed, the standard errors are then conditional on resamples in which they can be built, and the fit stops when fewer than half the replicates are usable. A cluster given with fe must nest the units (whole units are drawn; one that cuts across units is refused). The replicates are not jackknife-corrected.

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows, constant within a case); supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

nboot

Number of bootstrap refits for se = "bootstrap" (default 200).

cores

Number of parallel workers for the bootstrap (a PSOCK cluster; default 1). set.seed() before the call makes the resamples reproducible; serial and parallel runs use different random streams.

start

Optional starting values: the full parameter vector in the order of coef() but on the INTERNAL scale, which differs from coef() for the structural parameters (the logarithms of the inclusive values, scales, and standard deviations; the free Cholesky elements with a log diagonal for the multinomial probit covariance). object$theta of an earlier fit is on that scale. Rarely needed for mnl(), whose log-likelihood is globally concave; the other estimators start from the mnl() estimates (and imnl() from a multistart grid), so start serves to probe another basin of a non-concave likelihood.

maxit, reltol

Controls for the BFGS stage passed to stats::optim() (the plain mnl() is solved by damped Newton steps first, with BFGS as the fallback); the Newton polish that follows runs up to 25 further iterations with the analytic Hessian of the logit family or central differences of the analytic gradient otherwise.

draws

Number of GHK draws per case for four or more alternatives (default 200). The simulator's Halton sequences use one prime per dimension of the differenced utilities, the first 20, so the model takes at most 21 alternatives.

Value

An object of class c("mnprobit", "choicemodel").

Details

Only utility differences are identified. The model is parameterized through the covariance of the differences from the base alternative, \(\eta_k = \epsilon_k - \epsilon_b\), \(\tilde\Sigma = LL'\) with \(L\) lower triangular, its first element fixed at 1 (the scale normalization) and the remaining \(J(J-1)/2 - 1\) elements free (Train 2009, section 5.2; the same normalization as mlogit). The reported structural parameters are the elements of \(\tilde\Sigma\) named "var:<alt>" and "cov:<alt>,<alt>", with delta-method standard errors.

Probabilities: with three alternatives the exact bivariate normal (the Drezner-Genz algorithm, absolute error about 1e-15); with more, the GHK simulator with draws Halton draws per case, held fixed across evaluations (the simulated log-likelihood is smooth away from a singular covariance; the simulation error of a probability has standard deviation of order \(1/\sqrt{R}\) and the bias of its logarithm is of order \(1/R\), both vanishing with the number of draws; GHK probabilities of a case need not sum exactly to one, and the draws of a case are tied to its row position, so predictions for the same case in another row use other draws). Gradients are analytic throughout, including the covariance parameters (forward-mode differentiation through the Cholesky factor and the GHK recursion); the Hessian is obtained by central differences of the analytic gradient. The multinomial probit does not nest the multinomial logit, so compare them with vuong() or the information criteria. Multinomial probit coefficients are on a smaller scale than multinomial logit coefficients (the error-difference variance is normalized to 1 rather than \(\pi^2/3\)). Starting values come from the multinomial logit fit (scaled) with the covariance implied by iid errors, and from independent differences. Everything else is as in mnl(), except that the returned object has class "mnprobit" (not "mnp", which the CRAN package MNP uses).

Identification. With case-specific covariates only (alternative-specific coefficients, the wide layout) the covariance parameters are identified solely through the functional form and are fragile (Keane 1992): the likelihood is nearly flat along directions where an alternative's coefficients and its error variance shrink together, fits may stop at a near-singular covariance with a convergence warning, and the covariance estimates are not to be interpreted. Alternative-specific covariates with generic coefficients (the long layout) identify the covariance; a fit with a variance running to zero is flagged as a boundary fit. Near a singular covariance the GHK simulated likelihood is not smooth: with the draws held fixed, one draw's contribution can jump over a small change in the parameters, so a boundary fit with four or more alternatives may stop with a large gradient, and the boundary warning says that the convergence check is unreliable there.

References

Daganzo, C. (1979). Multinomial Probit: The Theory and Its Application to Demand Forecasting. New York: Academic Press.

Hausman, J.A. and Wise, D.A. (1978). A conditional probit model for qualitative choice. Econometrica, 46, 403-426. doi:10.2307/1913909

Train, K.E. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation, 2nd ed., chapter 5.

Keane, M.P. (1992). A note on identification in the multinomial probit model. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 10, 193-200. doi:10.1080/07350015.1992.10509898

See also

mnl(), nlogit(), hev(), vuong()

Other estimators: hev(), imnl(), mnl(), nlogit(), remnl(), rologit()

Examples

set.seed(5)
d <- rmnp(1500, beta = cbind(b = c(0.3, -0.6, 0.5), c = c(-0.2, 0.4, -0.3)),
          sigma = matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1.5), 2), gamma = 1)
m <- mnprobit(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = d, id = "id", alt = "alt")
summary(m)
